newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian rubber prices ease on low auto demand.
newsitem.headline: Indian rubber prices ease on low auto demand.

text.p: Indian rubber prices, despite low supplies, have crashed in the local markets on weak demand from the automobile sector, industry officials and traders said on Friday.
"The automobile industry is silent," said George Thomas, a leading dealer in the southern city of Coonoor.

Traders said rubber was currently quoted at 34-37 rupees per kg compared with 51.25 rupees at the same time last year. Earlier this week the government asked the State Trading Corporation to intervene in the market to check the sharp fall in prices.
They said rubber prices had shown a decline since June. The prices fell to 40.50 rupees on July 1 from 44.25 a month ago.
Traders said domestic supplies were thin with monsoon rains seriously disrupting tapping operations.
Growers said the demand for domestically produced rubber had fallen sharply after the government allowed the import of used tyres in its Export-Import policy earlier this year.
"The import of old tyres is affecting our livelihood," said Kurian Varghese, a rubber grower.
Growers said they have urged the government to use rubber in other areas like building of roads to increase its demand.

"Roads construction by mixing latex powder with tar has been found effective in various parts of (the southern state of) Kerala," said Vamadevan Nair, president of the Small Rubbers Farmers' Association.
Nair said rubber farmers had suffered losses to the extent of 10 billion rupees in the current season due to the fall in prices against rising input costs.

The Chief Minister of Kerala E.K. Nayanar has urged the federal government to raise the import duty on rubber. "There is a need to check imports because with recession, the domestic rubber is remaining unsold," Nayanar told the state assembly.
Thomas said imported rubber was about six rupees a kg cheaper than the domestically produced rubber.
A spokesman of the All India Rubber Industry Association (AIRIA) said that the government should allow free imports of rubber as the global prices were lower.
"Now that the world prices are lower, we should be allowed to import rubber and stock it," the spokesman said.
The state-run Rubber Board has revised its rubber output projection for 1997/98 (April-March) to 585,000 tonnes from 579,000 tonnes. It has estimated consumption at 619,000 tonnes.
The industry estimates that 1997/98 output would not be more than 579,000 tonnes but consumption would grow to about 632,000 tonnes.
"There will be a shortage of about 53,000 tonnes when the year ends," the AIRIA spokesman said. "So free imports when the prices are advantageous is logical."
